dialogue.speaker: Prof. Bohrlin
dialogue.text: Welcome to the Elemental Reaches, young chemist. Æquor is unravelling — but every atom still obeys the rules. Shall I refresh you?

choices.label: I know this — let me through.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Bohrlin
dialogue.text: An atom has a tiny, dense NUCLEUS — protons (+1) and neutrons (0) — surrounded by electrons (−1) in SHELLS.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Bohrlin
dialogue.text: The number of protons is the ATOMIC NUMBER — it decides which element you have. Protons + neutrons = MASS NUMBER.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Bohrlin
dialogue.text: Shells fill up: 2 in the first, then 8, then 8. The OUTER-shell electrons — the valence electrons — decide how an element reacts.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Bohrlin
dialogue.text: When you use a chemistry Skill in battle you'll be asked about this. Get it right and the reaction roars; get it wrong and I'll set you straight — no harm done. Off you go.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Bohrlin
dialogue.text: Confident! Then prove it in battle. Remember — a wrong answer just fizzles the move; it never hurts you.

dialogue.speaker: Archivist Mendel
dialogue.text: The Periodic Table is a map of every element — and it's been scrambled by the corruption. Let me show you how to read it.

dialogue.speaker: Archivist Mendel
dialogue.text: ROWS are PERIODS — going across, each atom gains a proton and an electron. COLUMNS are GROUPS — elements in a group have the same number of valence electrons, so they behave alike.

dialogue.speaker: Archivist Mendel
dialogue.text: Group 1 — alkali metals — one outer electron, fiercely reactive. Group 17 — halogens — need one more, also reactive. Group 18 — noble gases — full shells, almost inert.

dialogue.speaker: Archivist Mendel
dialogue.text: ISOTOPES are atoms of the same element with different neutron counts — same chemistry, different mass. An ION is an atom that's gained or lost electrons, so it carries a charge.

dialogue.speaker: Archivist Mendel
dialogue.text: Master this and the Unstable Isotope guarding the heart of this region won't stand a chance. Good luck.

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Quanta
dialogue.text: Behind me lies the Challenge Shrine — a gauntlet of questions, no monsters. Clear it and you'll earn an Energy Cell and a Stable Isotope Core.

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Quanta
dialogue.text: Six questions. Miss no more than one. Begin when ready.

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Quanta
dialogue.text: The Shrine will wait. Come back when you've studied.

dialogue.speaker: Master Smith Valentia
dialogue.text: So — you cleared the Reaches. Good. But the Forge is where atoms learn to HOLD ON to one another. Want the basics, or are you ready to forge?

choices.label: I know bonding — let me forge.

dialogue.speaker: Master Smith Valentia
dialogue.text: Atoms bond to fill their outer shells — to copy a noble gas. METALS have spare outer electrons; NON-METALS have spaces. Put them together and electrons MOVE.

dialogue.speaker: Master Smith Valentia
dialogue.text: That's an IONIC bond. The metal hands its electrons over and becomes a positive CATION; the non-metal takes them and becomes a negative ANION. Opposite charges lock into a giant LATTICE.

dialogue.speaker: Master Smith Valentia
dialogue.text: Ionic compounds are hard, brittle, and melt at high temperatures. Solid, they don't conduct — the ions are pinned. But molten, or dissolved in water, the ions are free to move, so they DO conduct.

dialogue.speaker: Master Smith Valentia
dialogue.text: Metals bond differently again: a lattice of positive ions in a SEA of loose, delocalised electrons. That sea is why metals conduct, why they bend instead of shatter, why they shine. Now — to the anvil.

dialogue.speaker: Master Smith Valentia
dialogue.text: Confident! Then prove it on the corrupted bonds ahead. Remember — a wrong answer just fizzles the move; it never hurts you. Go.

dialogue.speaker: Lorekeeper Octet
dialogue.text: Valentia bangs metal; I keep the rule that governs it all — the OCTET RULE. Eight electrons in the outer shell and an atom is content. Listen.

dialogue.speaker: Lorekeeper Octet
dialogue.text: When TWO NON-METALS meet, neither will give up electrons — so they SHARE. A shared pair is a COVALENT bond. Share two pairs and that's a double bond; three, a triple.

dialogue.speaker: Lorekeeper Octet
dialogue.text: Covalent atoms clump into small MOLECULES — H₂O, CO₂, O₂. The bonds INSIDE a molecule are strong, but molecules barely cling to one another, so these substances melt and boil low — many are gases or liquids — and they don't conduct.

dialogue.speaker: Lorekeeper Octet
dialogue.text: Why bond at all? Because a full outer shell is stable — the noble-gas configuration. Ionic, covalent, metallic: three roads, one destination.

dialogue.speaker: Lorekeeper Octet
dialogue.text: One last thing: some ions travel in packs — SO₄²⁻ sulfate, NO₃⁻ nitrate, CO₃²⁻ carbonate, OH⁻ hydroxide, NH₄⁺ ammonium. Treat each pack as one charged unit when you write a formula. Now go.

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Mortar
dialogue.text: The Mortar Shrine — no monsters, just questions on bonding. Clear it and you'll carry off an Energy Cell and a fresh Buffer. Step in?

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Mortar
dialogue.text: Six questions. One slip is forgiven; two and the Shrine spits you out. Begin when ready.

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Mortar
dialogue.text: The Shrine is patient. Study, then return.

dialogue.speaker: Alchemist Vera
dialogue.text: Reaction Hollow. Down here every reaction has a SHAPE — once you see the shape you can name it, and once you can name it you can use it. Want the shapes, or have you classified reactions before?

choices.label: I've classified reactions — let me through.

dialogue.speaker: Alchemist Vera
dialogue.text: SYNTHESIS (combination): two things become one. A + B → AB. Iron + sulfur → iron sulfide; a metal + oxygen → a metal oxide. Reactants merge; one product comes out.

dialogue.speaker: Alchemist Vera
dialogue.text: DECOMPOSITION: one thing becomes two. AB → A + B. Heat a metal carbonate and it gives a metal oxide + CO₂; run a current through water and it splits into H₂ + O₂.

dialogue.speaker: Alchemist Vera
dialogue.text: PRECIPITATION: mix two solutions and an insoluble solid drops out — we mark it with ↓ or (s). Silver nitrate + sodium chloride gives a white silver-chloride precipitate. A solid appears from two clear liquids.

dialogue.speaker: Alchemist Vera
dialogue.text: That's three of the five shapes. Pyrologist Ignis, further up, keeps the other two — COMBUSTION and DISPLACEMENT. Learn all five and the Eternal Flame won't fool you. Off you go.

dialogue.speaker: Alchemist Vera
dialogue.text: Confident! Then name the corrupted reactions up ahead as you fight them. Remember — a wrong answer just fizzles the move; it never hurts you. Go.

dialogue.speaker: Pyrologist Ignis
dialogue.text: Vera gave you the quiet shapes. I keep the loud ones. First: COMBUSTION.

dialogue.speaker: Pyrologist Ignis
dialogue.text: COMBUSTION: a fuel reacts with oxygen, releasing heat and light — it's EXOTHERMIC. Burn a hydrocarbon completely and you get carbon dioxide + water. Starve it of oxygen and you get carbon monoxide and soot instead.

dialogue.speaker: Pyrologist Ignis
dialogue.text: DISPLACEMENT: a more reactive metal kicks a less reactive one out of its compound. Zinc + copper sulfate → zinc sulfate + copper — the copper plates out as metal.

dialogue.speaker: Pyrologist Ignis
dialogue.text: How do you know which way it goes? The REACTIVITY SERIES: K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Cu, Ag, Au — high displaces low. Magnesium displaces copper; copper can't displace magnesium. The same rule tells you which metals rust or fizz in acid.

dialogue.speaker: Pyrologist Ignis
dialogue.text: Combustion, displacement — plus Vera's synthesis, decomposition, precipitation. Five shapes. The Flame at the top of the Hollow is combustion gone wild; classify it and you can quench it. Go.

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Cinder
dialogue.text: The Cinder Shrine — no monsters, just questions on reaction types. Clear it and you'll carry off an Energy Cell and a fresh Buffer. Step in?

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Cinder
dialogue.text: Six questions. One miss is forgiven; two and the embers spit you out. Begin when ready.

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Cinder
dialogue.text: The Shrine keeps its embers warm. Come back when you've studied.

dialogue.speaker: Archivist Pollux
dialogue.text: The Balance Halls. Here, an equation that doesn't balance simply won't work — the magic refuses it. Want the rules, or can you balance equations already?

choices.label: I can balance equations — let me through.

dialogue.speaker: Archivist Pollux
dialogue.text: Rule one — the LAW OF CONSERVATION OF MASS: in a reaction, atoms are only rearranged, never created or destroyed. So the total mass before equals the total mass after. If mass seems to vanish, a gas escaped — collect it and it's all still there.

dialogue.speaker: Archivist Pollux
dialogue.text: Rule two — write the SYMBOLS first. Turn each name into its formula: 'methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water' becomes CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O. THEN you balance it.

dialogue.speaker: Archivist Pollux
dialogue.text: Rule three — STATE SYMBOLS: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water. They tell you what form each substance is in — and (g) is why open containers seem to 'lose' mass.

dialogue.speaker: Archivist Pollux
dialogue.text: And once it's balanced, READ it as a ratio: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O means '2 of these react with 1 of those to make 2 of these'. Weighmaster Libra further up drills the actual balancing. Off you go.

dialogue.speaker: Archivist Pollux
dialogue.text: Confident! Then balance the warped equations roaming the Halls as you fight them. Remember — a wrong answer just fizzles the move; it never hurts you. Go.

dialogue.speaker: Weighmaster Libra
dialogue.text: Pollux gave you the laws. I give you the method. Listen close.

dialogue.speaker: Weighmaster Libra
dialogue.text: THE GOLDEN RULE: balance with COEFFICIENTS — the big numbers in FRONT of formulae. NEVER change a subscript (the little number inside). Changing H₂O to H₂O₂ doesn't balance anything — it makes a different chemical.

dialogue.speaker: Weighmaster Libra
dialogue.text: THE METHOD: count each element on both sides. Pick one that's unequal, put a coefficient in front to fix it, then re-count everything. Repeat. Save the awkward element — often oxygen, or hydrogen — for last.

dialogue.speaker: Weighmaster Libra
dialogue.text: A SHORTCUT: if a polyatomic ion — SO₄, NO₃, OH — survives the reaction intact, balance it as a single chunk instead of element by element. Less counting, fewer mistakes.

dialogue.speaker: Weighmaster Libra
dialogue.text: Worked example: __Fe + __O₂ → __Fe₂O₃. Fe₂O₃ has 2 Fe and 3 O. Try 2 of it → 4 Fe and 6 O → so 4 Fe and 3 O₂ on the left. Answer: 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃. The Lopsided Equation at the top of the Halls has never once balanced. Go and balance it.

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Scale
dialogue.text: The Scale Shrine — no monsters, just questions on conservation and balancing. Clear it and you'll carry off an Energy Cell and a fresh Buffer. Step in?

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Scale
dialogue.text: Six questions. One miss is forgiven; two and the scales tip you out. Begin when ready.

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Scale
dialogue.text: The scales hold steady. Come back when you've practised.

dialogue.speaker: Kineticist Vasco
dialogue.text: Catalyst Crags — where everything wants to go FAST. Down here a reaction either crawls or runs away; there's no in-between unless you control the levers. Want the levers, or do you know your reaction rates already?

choices.label: I know reaction rates — let me through.

dialogue.speaker: Kineticist Vasco
dialogue.text: It all comes down to COLLISIONS. A reaction only happens when particles smack into each other hard enough — and lined up the right way. More collisions, harder collisions, faster reaction. Simple as that.

dialogue.speaker: Kineticist Vasco
dialogue.text: Lever one — TEMPERATURE. Heat it up: particles move faster, so they collide more often AND a far bigger share of those collisions have enough punch to react. A modest rise can speed things up a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Kineticist Vasco
dialogue.text: Lever two — CONCENTRATION (and PRESSURE for gases). Cram more particles into the same space and they bump into each other more often per second. More crowded, faster reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Kineticist Vasco
dialogue.text: That's two of the levers. Chemurge Sela further up keeps the other two — SURFACE AREA and CATALYSTS. Learn all four and the Runaway Reaction at the top can't outpace you. Off you go.

dialogue.speaker: Kineticist Vasco
dialogue.text: Confident! Then keep up with the things racing around the Crags. Remember — a wrong answer just fizzles the move; it never hurts you. Go.

dialogue.speaker: Chemurge Sela
dialogue.text: Vasco gave you heat and concentration. I hold the other two levers — and the trick for spotting how fast a reaction really is.

dialogue.speaker: Chemurge Sela
dialogue.text: Lever three — SURFACE AREA. Only matters for a solid. Break it up — better yet, powder it — and you expose vastly more surface for the other reactant to collide with. A marble chip in acid just sits there; powdered marble fizzes furiously.

dialogue.speaker: Chemurge Sela
dialogue.text: Lever four — CATALYSTS. A catalyst gives the reaction a shortcut: a pathway needing LESS energy to get going, so more collisions succeed. And it's NOT used up — a pinch of it works again and again. ENZYMES are nature's catalysts. A catalyst changes the SPEED, never the amount of product.

dialogue.speaker: Chemurge Sela
dialogue.text: And to MEASURE the rate: collect the gas given off against time, or weigh the flask as gas escapes, or time a cross vanishing under a forming precipitate. On a graph, a STEEPER line means faster — and the line flattens the moment a reactant runs out.

dialogue.speaker: Chemurge Sela
dialogue.text: Collisions, temperature, concentration, surface area, catalysts — five hands on the throttle. The Runaway Reaction has pulled every one of them. Go and slow it down.

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Tally
dialogue.text: The Tally Shrine — no monsters, just questions on what makes reactions fast or slow. Clear it and you'll carry off an Energy Cell and a fresh Buffer. Step in?

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Tally
dialogue.text: Six questions. One miss is forgiven; two and the stopwatch stops you. Begin when ready.

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Tally
dialogue.text: The stopwatch is always ready. Come back when you've studied.

dialogue.speaker: Apothecary Vitra
dialogue.text: The Acid Wastes. Everything here is either eating something or being eaten — that's pH for you. Want the chemistry of acids and bases, or do you know it?

choices.label: I know acids and bases — let me through.

dialogue.speaker: Apothecary Vitra
dialogue.text: What makes an acid an ACID: in water it releases H⁺ — hydrogen ions. A BASE releases OH⁻ — hydroxide ions. A base that dissolves in water is an ALKALI. That single difference — H⁺ versus OH⁻ — is the whole story.

dialogue.speaker: Apothecary Vitra
dialogue.text: The pH SCALE runs 0 to 14. Below 7 = acidic, 7 = neutral, above 7 = alkaline. The LOWER the number, the more acidic — and each step is roughly a tenfold change in how acidic.

dialogue.speaker: Apothecary Vitra
dialogue.text: INDICATORS read the pH for you. LITMUS: red in acid, blue in alkali. UNIVERSAL INDICATOR: a whole rainbow — red→orange→yellow→green→blue→purple from strong acid to strong alkali. pH paper or a pH meter give you a number.

dialogue.speaker: Apothecary Vitra
dialogue.text: And mind the wording: STRONG vs WEAK is about how FULLY the acid ionises; DILUTE vs CONCENTRATED is just about how much WATER is in it. Two different things. Salter Mordant up ahead has neutralisation and naming salts. Off you go.

dialogue.speaker: Apothecary Vitra
dialogue.text: Confident! Then handle the corrosive things prowling the Wastes. Remember — a wrong answer just fizzles the move; it never hurts you. Go.

dialogue.speaker: Salter Mordant
dialogue.text: Vitra told you what acids and bases ARE. I'll show you what they DO to each other.

dialogue.speaker: Salter Mordant
dialogue.text: NEUTRALISATION: acid + base → SALT + WATER. The H⁺ from the acid grabs the OH⁻ from the base and they make water; whatever's left over pairs up to form the salt. Add just enough base and the pH lands on 7.

dialogue.speaker: Salter Mordant
dialogue.text: Acids react with more than bases. Acid + reactive METAL → salt + HYDROGEN (the gas that pops). Acid + metal CARBONATE → salt + water + CARBON DIOXIDE (fizzes, turns limewater milky). Acid + metal OXIDE → salt + water.

dialogue.speaker: Salter Mordant
dialogue.text: NAMING the salt: the metal part comes from the BASE; the rest comes from the ACID. HYDROCHLORIC acid → chlorides. SULFURIC acid → sulfates. NITRIC acid → nitrates. So sodium hydroxide + hydrochloric acid → sodium chloride.

dialogue.speaker: Salter Mordant
dialogue.text: Acids, bases, pH, indicators, neutralisation, salts — that's the full kit. The pH Tyrant at the top of the Wastes has dragged everything down to pH 0. Go and neutralise it.

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Litmus
dialogue.text: The Litmus Shrine — no monsters, just questions on acids, bases and neutralisation. Clear it and you'll carry off an Energy Cell and a fresh Buffer. Step in?

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Litmus
dialogue.text: Six questions. One miss is forgiven; two and the indicator turns you out. Begin when ready.

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Litmus
dialogue.text: The litmus paper waits. Come back when you've studied.

dialogue.speaker: Thermologist Calor
dialogue.text: The Crucible. Every reaction here either gives out heat or drinks it in — never neither. Want me to walk you through energy changes, or do you already know them?

choices.label: I know energy changes — let me through.

dialogue.speaker: Thermologist Calor
dialogue.text: Two kinds. EXOTHERMIC: energy is RELEASED to the surroundings, so they warm UP — the products end up LOWER in energy than the reactants, and we say ΔH is NEGATIVE. ENDOTHERMIC: energy is TAKEN IN from the surroundings, so they cool DOWN — products end up HIGHER in energy, ΔH is POSITIVE.

dialogue.speaker: Thermologist Calor
dialogue.text: Why? Look at the bonds. BREAKING a bond always ABSORBS energy (that step is endothermic). MAKING a bond always RELEASES energy (that step is exothermic). The overall change is just the BALANCE: if making the new bonds releases more than breaking the old ones cost, it's exothermic overall — and the other way round for endothermic.

dialogue.speaker: Thermologist Calor
dialogue.text: Draw it as a REACTION PROFILE: reactants on the left, products on the right, and a HUMP between them. The height of the hump above the reactants is the ACTIVATION ENERGY — the minimum energy a collision needs before the reaction can happen at all. A CATALYST gives a lower path: it shrinks the hump, but it does NOT move the start or end heights, so it never changes ΔH.

dialogue.speaker: Thermologist Calor
dialogue.text: Exo gives heat out, endo takes it in; bonds break in, make out; the profile shows the activation hump. That's the whole map. Forgemaster Pyra up ahead has the everyday examples. Go on.

dialogue.speaker: Thermologist Calor
dialogue.text: Confident, then. Mind the things prowling the forge floor — a wrong answer just fizzles your move, it never burns you. Off you go.

dialogue.speaker: Forgemaster Pyra
dialogue.text: Calor gave you the theory. I'll show you where you've already met it.

dialogue.speaker: Forgemaster Pyra
dialogue.text: EXOTHERMIC, everywhere: any COMBUSTION — fuels burning in the forge; RESPIRATION in your own cells; chemical HAND-WARMERS; NEUTRALISATION of an acid with a base; and most OXIDATIONS, even rusting. Touch the flask afterwards — it's HOT. Heat flowed OUT.

dialogue.speaker: Forgemaster Pyra
dialogue.text: ENDOTHERMIC, also everywhere: THERMAL DECOMPOSITION — you must keep heating a carbonate to break it apart; PHOTOSYNTHESIS, which stores light energy; DISSOLVING certain salts, the trick behind an instant COLD PACK; and ELECTROLYSIS. Touch that flask and it's gone COLD. Heat flowed IN.

dialogue.speaker: Forgemaster Pyra
dialogue.text: How to tell which, in the lab: do it in a POLYSTYRENE CUP and watch the thermometer. Temperature goes UP → exothermic, ΔH negative. Temperature goes DOWN → endothermic, ΔH positive. The cup just stops the heat leaking, so the reading is honest.

dialogue.speaker: Forgemaster Pyra
dialogue.text: Examples, the cup test, the sign of ΔH — that's the practical half. The Heat Sink waits past the gate above. It pulls heat out of everything near it — go and put the balance right.

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Ember
dialogue.text: The Ember Shrine — no monsters, only questions on energy changes: exo and endo, bond energy, reaction profiles. Clear it and you'll carry off an Energy Cell and a fresh Buffer. Step in?

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Ember
dialogue.text: Six questions. One miss is forgiven; two and the coals go cold on you. Begin when you're ready.

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Ember
dialogue.text: The embers will keep. Come back when you've studied.

dialogue.speaker: Equilibrist Lethe
dialogue.text: Equilibrium's Heart — where every reaction runs both ways at once. The Great Imbalance tipped the scales in one direction and locked them there. Shall I walk you through what equilibrium actually means, or do you already know it?

choices.label: I know equilibrium — let me through.

dialogue.speaker: Equilibrist Lethe
dialogue.text: Start with the ⇌ symbol — two arrows, each pointing a different way. A REVERSIBLE reaction doesn't go fully to products and stop. Instead it reaches EQUILIBRIUM: the forward and reverse reactions are still both happening, but at equal rates, so the amounts of everything stop changing.

dialogue.speaker: Equilibrist Lethe
dialogue.text: DYNAMIC equilibrium: the reaction is NOT stopped — both directions are ongoing. Macroscopic properties (colour, pressure, concentration) appear constant because the rates balance. It only holds in a CLOSED system where nothing can escape.

dialogue.speaker: Equilibrist Lethe
dialogue.text: Le Châtelier's Principle: if you disturb an equilibrium, it shifts to partially OPPOSE that change. Add more reactant → equilibrium shifts RIGHT (makes more product). Remove product → shifts right again. Change concentration the other way and it reverses.

dialogue.speaker: Equilibrist Lethe
dialogue.text: Temperature: raise it → equilibrium shifts in the ENDOTHERMIC direction (to absorb the extra heat). Lower it → shifts EXOTHERMIC. This also changes the position permanently — unlike pressure or concentration, temperature changes the equilibrium constant itself.

dialogue.speaker: Equilibrist Lethe
dialogue.text: Pressure (gases only): raise pressure → equilibrium shifts to the side with FEWER gas moles, reducing the pressure. Lower pressure → shifts to the side with MORE moles. If both sides have the same number of gas moles, pressure has no effect.

dialogue.speaker: Equilibrist Lethe
dialogue.text: CATALYST: it speeds up both the forward AND reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but the POSITION does NOT change. The yield is unaffected. A catalyst NEVER shifts the equilibrium.

dialogue.speaker: Equilibrist Lethe
dialogue.text: Examples: the HABER process — N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ — exothermic, high pressure (fewer gas moles on the right) and a moderate temperature (200°C with catalyst) balances yield vs rate. The CONTACT process for sulfuric acid works the same way. Fizzy drinks: CO₂ dissolved under pressure; open the can, pressure drops, equilibrium shifts left — CO₂ bubbles out.

dialogue.speaker: Equilibrist Lethe
dialogue.text: That's equilibrium. The Great Imbalance beyond the gate is Catalyst affinity — no matchup will save you; bring your refined skills and keep the chain alive. Go restore it.

dialogue.speaker: Equilibrist Lethe
dialogue.text: Confident — and this is the right place for it. Remember: a wrong answer in battle just fizzles the move, never hurts you. The Great Imbalance is Catalyst affinity, so no type advantage exists. Go.

dialogue.speaker: Warden Haldane
dialogue.text: You made it this far. Good. I've been watching the Heart since the Great Imbalance sealed the gate — it's unlike anything in the other regions.

dialogue.speaker: Warden Haldane
dialogue.text: It's Catalyst affinity. That means the type chart gives you nothing — no matchup bonus, no super-effective strike. The Great Imbalance answers to no element. Don't waste your turn fishing for a weakness that isn't there.

dialogue.speaker: Warden Haldane
dialogue.text: What WILL carry you through: refined skills at high tiers, the chain meter built and kept alive, and your Reagents saved for when its HP drops into the final quarter. It hits hard and has a buff-strip move — watch for Equilibrate clearing your boosts.

dialogue.speaker: Warden Haldane
dialogue.text: The miniboss ahead — The Forward Drift — is Synthesis affinity. Your Decomposition skills will shred it. Use that fight to top up your chain meter before you face the gate. Then go finish what the rest of Æquor couldn't.

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Cyra
dialogue.text: The Heart Shrine — no enemies, only six questions on equilibrium: reversible reactions, dynamic equilibrium, Le Châtelier. Clear it and you'll carry off a Reagent and an Isotope Core. Step in?

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Cyra
dialogue.text: Six questions. One miss is forgiven; two and the balance tips against you. Begin when you're ready.

dialogue.speaker: Shrinekeeper Cyra
dialogue.text: The Shrine holds steady. Come back when you've studied the equilibrium concepts.

dialogue.speaker: Vendor Mara
dialogue.text: Atoms are everywhere — and so is quality gear. I stock reagent equipment for chemists heading into the Reaches. Browse what I have?

dialogue.speaker: Vendor Mara
dialogue.text: Curie's Cache — only the finest forge-tested equipment. Choose carefully.

dialogue.speaker: Vendor Mara
dialogue.text: I'll be here. The Reaches wait for no one, but I do.

dialogue.speaker: Merchant Rho
dialogue.text: The Forge hammers day and night, and so do I. Good equipment makes the difference between a clean bond and a broken one. Care to browse?

dialogue.speaker: Merchant Rho
dialogue.text: The Bonded Vault — gear bound to last. Step inside.

dialogue.speaker: Merchant Rho
dialogue.text: The vault is always unlocked. Come back when you're ready.

dialogue.speaker: Trader Kira
dialogue.text: Every reaction leaves a residue — and the best ones leave behind fine equipment. I collect and sell them here in Reaction Hollow. Interested?

dialogue.speaker: Trader Kira
dialogue.text: Hollow Reagents — good gear for hungry chemists. Have a look.

dialogue.speaker: Trader Kira
dialogue.text: Suit yourself. I'll still be here after you fight.

dialogue.speaker: Vendor Theron
dialogue.text: Every equation has two sides, and every chemist needs two things: knowledge and equipment. I supply the second. Want to take a look?

dialogue.speaker: Vendor Theron
dialogue.text: The Balanced Scales — precisely curated gear. Choose your side.

dialogue.speaker: Vendor Theron
dialogue.text: The scales tip for no one. Come back when you've decided.

dialogue.speaker: Merchant Vex
dialogue.text: Catalyst Crags run fast — so does my business. Everything I carry accelerates your edge. Want to see?

dialogue.speaker: Merchant Vex
dialogue.text: Crag Merchants — mid-tier gear for mid-tier threats. Don't wait.

dialogue.speaker: Merchant Vex
dialogue.text: Speed is everything here. Don't wait too long.

dialogue.speaker: Trader Osh
dialogue.text: Acid eats through most things, but good equipment resists. I've seen what happens when chemists come through without proper gear. Don't let that be you. Want to browse?

dialogue.speaker: Trader Osh
dialogue.text: The Neutralised Stock — gear that balances the pH of danger. Choose well.

dialogue.speaker: Trader Osh
dialogue.text: Your confidence is admirable. Misplaced, perhaps. Come back if you change your mind.

dialogue.speaker: Vendor Brix
dialogue.text: The Crucible tests everything — metal, bond, and chemist alike. My gear is forged right here in the heat. It holds. Want to see what we have?

dialogue.speaker: Vendor Brix
dialogue.text: The Crucible Forge — T2 and T3 equipment, tested in real heat. Make your choice.

dialogue.speaker: Vendor Brix
dialogue.text: The forge stays hot. Come back when you need it.

dialogue.speaker: Merchant Mira
dialogue.text: Equilibrium's Heart holds the final balance of Æquor. You'll want every advantage you can get. Let me show you what the Heart Market has to offer.

dialogue.speaker: Merchant Mira
dialogue.text: Heart Market — finest equipment in Æquor. Take what you need.

dialogue.speaker: Merchant Mira
dialogue.text: Courage. I respect that. I'll be here when you need me.
